rules.title: NSAID in Kidney Disease · Acute Renal Failure Risk
rules.clinicalText: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin E2 synthesis, precipitating pre-renal vasoconstriction, acute interstitial nephritis, and acceleration of chronic kidney disease.
rules.plainText: You have kidney issues and are taking an NSAID pain reliever. NSAIDs reduce blood flow to your kidneys and can cause acute kidney injury or worsening kidney disease.
rules.rationale: Inhibition of vasodilatory renal prostaglandins causes abrupt reduction in glomerular filtration rate.

rules.title: Metformin in Renal Impairment · Lactic Acidosis Caution
rules.clinicalText: Metformin is cleared primarily by renal tubular secretion. Impaired eGFR increases plasma metformin concentrations, elevating the risk of potentially fatal lactic acidosis.
rules.plainText: You have kidney issues and take Metformin. If kidney function drops (eGFR below 30 mL/min), Metformin can build up and cause severe lactic acidosis. Regular kidney blood tests are required.
rules.rationale: Decreased renal elimination leads to toxic accumulation and suppression of hepatic gluconeogenesis.
rules.source: FDA Black Box Warning / STOPP/START v3

rules.title: Potassium-Sparing Diuretic in Kidney Disease · Severe Hyperkalemia
rules.clinicalText: Aldosterone antagonists inhibit renal potassium excretion; in existing renal impairment, severe life-threatening hyperkalemia (>6.0 mEq/L) and fatal cardiac arrhythmias can occur rapidly.
rules.plainText: Taking water pills that hold potassium (like Spironolactone) with kidney issues can cause potassium to spike dangerously high, risking sudden heart rhythm arrest.
rules.rationale: Impaired baseline glomerular filtration compounds drug-induced inhibition of distal tubular potassium secretion.

rules.title: Digoxin in Renal Dysfunction · Digitalis Toxicity
rules.clinicalText: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and 70-80% renal excretion. In renal impairment, accumulation triggers heart block, fatal ventricular arrhythmias, and visual disturbances.
rules.plainText: Digoxin is cleared by your kidneys. Because you have kidney issues, Digoxin can easily build up to toxic levels, causing heart rhythm disturbances and nausea.
rules.rationale: Clearance correlates directly with creatinine clearance; doses > 0.125 mg/day strongly discouraged in impaired renal function.

rules.title: Sulfonylurea in Renal Impairment · Prolonged Hypoglycemia Risk
rules.clinicalText: Active metabolites of long-acting sulfonylureas accumulate in renal insufficiency, causing prolonged, severe, and potentially life-threatening hypoglycemia in older adults.
rules.plainText: Your diabetes medicine (sulfonylurea) takes longer to leave your body because of kidney impairment, causing sudden severe low blood sugar episodes.
rules.rationale: Decreased clearance of active metabolites causes sustained stimulation of pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion.

rules.title: Lithium in Renal Impairment · Acute Neurotoxicity
rules.clinicalText: Lithium is 100% renally excreted. Reduced renal filtration rapidly precipitates systemic lithium toxicity characterized by coarse tremor, ataxia, convulsions, and irreversible nephrotoxicity.
rules.plainText: Lithium levels depend entirely on kidney clearance. With kidney impairment, dangerous toxic levels build up quickly.
rules.rationale: Narrow therapeutic window and purely renal elimination.

rules.title: Methotrexate in Renal Dysfunction · Bone Marrow Suppression
rules.clinicalText: Methotrexate clearance depends on glomerular filtration. In renal impairment, systemic exposure increases exponentially, causing profound myelosuppression and severe mucositis.
rules.plainText: Methotrexate can cause life-threatening blood and marrow toxicity if kidneys cannot clear it rapidly.
rules.rationale: Impaired excretion leads to sustained high free-drug levels inhibiting dihydrofolate reductase in non-target tissues.

rules.title: SGLT2 Inhibitor with Reduced Kidney Function · Glycemic Efficacy Alert
rules.clinicalText: SGLT2 inhibitors depend on filtered glucose load for glycemic efficacy; while renoprotective in CKD, blood-sugar lowering declines markedly when eGFR < 45 mL/min.
rules.plainText: Your SGLT2 diabetes medicine protects kidney and heart health, but its blood-sugar lowering strength weakens if kidney filtration is low.
rules.rationale: Mechanistic dependence on glomerular filtration for glucosuria.

rules.title: NSAID in Heart Failure · Acute Decompensation & Fluid Retention
rules.clinicalText: NSAIDs promote renal sodium and water retention, blunting loop diuretic responsiveness and triggering congestive heart failure exacerbation and hospitalizations.
rules.plainText: You have a heart condition and take an NSAID. NSAIDs cause your body to hold extra fluid, causing swollen legs and worsening shortness of breath or heart failure.
rules.rationale: Inhibition of renal prostaglandins results in sodium retention and systemic vascular resistance elevation.

rules.title: Non-Dihydropyridine CCB in Heart Failure · Negative Inotropic Collapse
rules.clinicalText: Verapamil and diltiazem possess potent negative inotropic properties that significantly depress left ventricular contractility, precipitating acute cardiogenic decompensation in systolic heart failure.
rules.plainText: Verapamil or Diltiazem weakens the squeezing power of your heart muscle, which can severely worsen congestive heart failure.
rules.rationale: Negative inotropic effect on myocardium with compromised ejection fraction.

rules.title: Amiodarone with Conduction Disease · Severe Bradycardia Risk
rules.clinicalText: Amiodarone depresses sinus node automaticity and AV conduction; in pre-existing bradycardia or sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker, complete AV block and asystole can occur.
rules.plainText: Amiodarone strongly slows your heart's electrical wiring. In patients with slow pulse or conduction defects, it can cause severe dizziness or fainting.
rules.rationale: Combined beta-blockade and calcium/potassium channel inhibition slows AV nodal conduction.

rules.title: Tricyclic Antidepressant in Heart Disease · QTc Prolongation & Arrhythmia
rules.clinicalText: TCAs possess quinidine-like Class IA antiarrhythmic actions, prolonging the QTc interval and precipitating fatal ventricular arrhythmias, orthostatic syncope, and tachycardia.
rules.plainText: Amitriptyline and related antidepressants affect heart electrical rhythms. In heart disease, they increase the danger of fainting and abnormal heartbeats.
rules.rationale: Sodium and potassium channel blockade extends myocardial repolarization times.

rules.title: Oral Decongestants in Heart Disease · Tachycardia & Ischemia
rules.clinicalText: Sympathomimetic vasoconstrictors cause reflex tachycardia and coronary vasoconstriction, increasing myocardial oxygen demand and precipitating angina or arrhythmias.
rules.plainText: Cold medicines with pseudoephedrine or phenylephrine stimulate the heart, causing fast palpitations and chest tightness in heart patients.
rules.rationale: Alpha-1 and beta-1 adrenergic stimulation elevates cardiac workload and myocardial oxygen consumption.
rules.source: AHA Advisory on OTC Cough/Cold Products

rules.title: Cholinesterase Inhibitor in Cardiac Conduction Disease · Syncope Alert
rules.clinicalText: Cholinesterase inhibitors enhance central and peripheral vagal tone, producing sinus bradycardia, sinoatrial block, syncope, and fall-related fractures in older adults.
rules.plainText: Dementia medications like Donepezil increase vagal nerve activity, which can slow your heart rate too much, causing lightheadedness and fainting spells.
rules.rationale: Vagomimetic action on sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes.

rules.title: Fluoroquinolone in Heart Disease · QTc Prolongation & Torsades
rules.clinicalText: Fluoroquinolones block the myocardial HERG potassium channel, prolonging ventricular repolarization and precipitating Torsades de Pointes, particularly in patients with baseline cardiac disease.
rules.plainText: This antibiotic can prolong the electrical reset of your heartbeat. In heart patients, this raises the risk of dangerous irregular heart rhythms.
rules.rationale: Blockade of rapid delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr).

rules.title: Macrolide in Cardiovascular Disease · Cardiac Mortality Signal
rules.clinicalText: Macrolide antibiotics delay cardiac repolarization and carry an established epidemiological signal for sudden cardiac death and acute coronary syndromes in patients with baseline CAD.
rules.plainText: Macrolide antibiotics (like Clarithromycin or Azithromycin) require caution in heart disease due to potential heart rhythm irregularities.
rules.rationale: IKr potassium channel inhibition and post-market epidemiological cardiovascular safety signals.
rules.source: FDA Safety Alert / NEJM Cardiovascular Warning

rules.title: NSAID in Hypertension · Blunted BP Control & Pressure Spikes
rules.clinicalText: NSAIDs antagonize the antihypertensive action of ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta-blockers, and diuretics, producing an average 3 to 6 mmHg increase in mean arterial pressure.
rules.plainText: You have high blood pressure and take an NSAID. NSAIDs counteract your blood pressure medicines, causing blood pressure to rise.
rules.rationale: Renal prostaglandin inhibition promotes systemic vasoconstriction and blunts natriuresis.
rules.source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023 / AHA Hypertension Guidelines

rules.title: Systemic Corticosteroid in Hypertension · Sodium Retention Alert
rules.clinicalText: Glucocorticoids possess mineralocorticoid activity, stimulating distal tubular sodium reabsorption and volume expansion, destabilizing blood pressure control.
rules.plainText: Steroids make your body retain salt and water, which can push your blood pressure up significantly. Monitor your blood pressure daily.
rules.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor activation leading to intravascular volume expansion.

rules.title: Oral Decongestant in Hypertension · Acute Vasoconstriction
rules.clinicalText: Alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation produces arterial smooth muscle contraction and peripheral vascular resistance elevation, potentially precipitating hypertensive crisis.
rules.plainText: Over-the-counter decongestants tighten your blood vessels and can cause dangerous blood pressure spikes in people with hypertension.
rules.rationale: Direct peripheral alpha-1 vasoconstriction.
rules.source: ACC/AHA Guideline for Prevention & Treatment of High Blood Pressure

rules.title: Licorice Supplement in Hypertension · Pseudohyperaldosteronism
rules.clinicalText: Glycyrrhizin inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, allowing cortisol to bind mineralocorticoid receptors, causing severe hypokalemia, sodium retention, and severe hypertension.
rules.plainText: Licorice root supplements block the enzyme that protects your kidneys from stress hormones, driving blood pressure up and wasting potassium.
rules.rationale: Inhibition of 11-beta-HSD2 produces apparent mineralocorticoid excess.

rules.title: Wakefulness Promoters in Hypertension · Sympathomimetic BP Elevation
rules.clinicalText: Central wakefulness agents elevate circulating catecholamines, producing mild-to-moderate sustained increases in systolic blood pressure and resting heart rate.
rules.plainText: Stimulant or wakefulness medicines can increase your blood pressure and heart rate. Frequent blood pressure checks are advised.
rules.rationale: Central monoaminergic stimulation elevating adrenergic tone.

rules.title: Systemic Corticosteroids in Diabetes · Severe Hyperglycemia Spikes
rules.clinicalText: Glucocorticoids induce acute peripheral insulin resistance, stimulate hepatic gluconeogenesis, and suppress pancreatic insulin release, causing severe steroid-induced hyperglycemia.
rules.plainText: Steroids dramatically raise blood sugar levels by making your body resist insulin. You will likely need to adjust your diabetes medication while on steroids.
rules.rationale: Up-regulation of phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase and glucose-6-phosphatase coupled with inhibition of GLUT4 translocation.
rules.source: American Diabetes Association (ADA) Standards of Care

rules.title: Non-Selective Beta-Blocker in Diabetes · Hypoglycemia Masking
rules.clinicalText: Beta-adrenergic antagonists blunt catecholamine-mediated warning symptoms of hypoglycemia (tremor, palpitations, anxiety), leaving diaphoresis as the sole identifiable sign.
rules.plainText: Beta-blockers can hide common warning signs of low blood sugar, such as shakiness and fast heartbeat, making low blood sugar harder to detect early.
rules.rationale: Sympathetic antagonism blunts physiological adrenergic response to falling blood glucose.
rules.source: ADA Standards of Care / STOPP Criteria

rules.title: Fluoroquinolone in Diabetes · Severe Dysglycemia Risk
rules.clinicalText: Fluoroquinolones interfere with pancreatic ATP-sensitive K+ channels, causing unpredictable, severe glycemic fluctuations ranging from profound hypoglycemia to diabetic ketoacidosis.
rules.plainText: This antibiotic can cause sudden severe drops or sharp spikes in blood sugar in diabetic patients. Monitor your glucose levels frequently.
rules.rationale: Direct modulation of pancreatic beta-cell potassium channels.
rules.source: FDA Drug Safety Communication on Fluoroquinolone Dysglycemia

rules.title: Second-Generation Antipsychotic in Diabetes · Metabolic Decompensation
rules.clinicalText: Olanzapine and clozapine produce substantial metabolic adverse effects, including profound weight gain, marked insulin resistance, and diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar coma.
rules.plainText: Antipsychotic medications like Olanzapine can cause significant weight gain and make diabetes much harder to control.
rules.rationale: Central 5-HT2C and H1 antagonism coupled with peripheral impairment of insulin secretion and sensitivity.
rules.source: ADA / APA Consensus on Antipsychotic Drugs and Diabetes

rules.title: Thiazide Diuretics in Diabetes · Impaired Glycemic Control
rules.clinicalText: Thiazide-induced hypokalemia impairs insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells, worsening HbA1c and glucose tolerance over long-term treatment.
rules.plainText: Thiazide water pills can slightly raise blood sugar by lowering potassium levels. Maintaining healthy potassium helps keep blood sugar steady.
rules.rationale: Hypokalemia blunts beta-cell membrane depolarization and insulin exocytosis.

rules.title: Benzodiazepine in Dementia · Delirium & Accelerated Decline
rules.clinicalText: Benzodiazepines exacerbate baseline cognitive impairment, induce delirium, produce anterograde amnesia, and significantly increase mortality and hospitalizations in patients with dementia.
rules.plainText: You or your family member has memory impairment or dementia. Benzodiazepines (calming pills) worsen confusion, memory loss, and can cause sudden delirium.
rules.rationale: GABA-A agonism worsens central cholinergic deficits in neurodegenerative disease.

rules.title: Potent Anticholinergic in Dementia · Severe Confusion & Toxidrome
rules.clinicalText: Dementia is characterized by profound central cholinergic deficits; anticholinergic medications directly antagonize remaining muscarinic receptors, causing acute delirium, hallucinations, and rapid cognitive deterioration.
rules.plainText: This medication has strong anticholinergic properties that block acetylcholine, the key chemical brain messenger for memory. In dementia, this causes severe confusion and hallucinations.
rules.rationale: Antagonism of central muscarinic receptors severely exacerbates cholinergic deficit.
rules.source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023 / STOPP Criteria v3

rules.title: Antipsychotic in Dementia · Black Box Warning for Mortality & Stroke
rules.clinicalText: Antipsychotics carry an FDA Black Box warning in dementia-related psychosis due to a 1.6- to 1.7-fold increase in all-cause mortality, predominantly from cardiovascular events and pneumonia, alongside stroke risk.
rules.plainText: Antipsychotic drugs carry an FDA warning when used in dementia because they significantly increase the danger of stroke and overall mortality. They should only be used as a last resort.
rules.rationale: Increased cerebrovascular events, sedation-related aspiration pneumonia, and accelerated cognitive loss.
rules.source: FDA Black Box Warning / AGS Beers Criteria 2023

rules.title: Z-Hypnotic in Dementia · Nighttime Wandering & Confusion
rules.clinicalText: Non-benzodiazepine receptor agonists worsen sleep architecture, trigger paradoxical excitement, sleepwalking, delirium, and nocturnal wandering in cognitively impaired elders.
rules.plainText: Sleeping pills like Zolpidem can cause severe night-time confusion, wandering, and dangerous falls in people with memory impairment.
rules.rationale: Selective alpha-1 GABA-A subunit agonism produces psychomotor impairment and amnesia.

rules.title: Tricyclic Antidepressant in Dementia · High Cognitive Burden
rules.clinicalText: High anticholinergic and sedative properties of TCAs severely impair memory consolidation and cause prominent daytime sedation in patients with cognitive impairment.
rules.plainText: Tricyclic antidepressants (like Amitriptyline) heavily impair memory and should be avoided in patients with dementia in favor of safer alternatives.
rules.rationale: High Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB score = 3) directly counteracts cognitive functioning.

rules.title: Skeletal Muscle Relaxant in Dementia · Sedation & Delirium
rules.clinicalText: Muscle relaxants possess central anticholinergic and depressant properties that are poorly tolerated in older adults with cognitive impairment, precipitating profound disorientation.
rules.plainText: Muscle relaxant medications cause heavy brain sedation and disorientation in older adults with memory issues.
rules.rationale: Central nervous system depression combined with peripheral and central anticholinergic activity.

rules.title: Antispasmodic in Dementia · Muscarinic Blockade Warning
rules.clinicalText: Tertiary amine antispasmodics readily cross the blood-brain barrier and cause acute delirium and severe constipation in patients with baseline dementia.
rules.plainText: Stomach cramp medicines like Dicyclomine easily cross into the brain and block memory function, causing acute confusion.
rules.rationale: Blood-brain barrier penetration with central antimuscarinic action.

rules.title: Benzodiazepine with Fall History · High Fracture & Ataxia Risk
rules.clinicalText: Benzodiazepines cause psychomotor slowing, prolonged reaction times, vestibular dysfunction, and daytime drowsiness, increasing the risk of falls and hip fractures by 50-100% in older adults.
rules.plainText: You have a history of falls and take a calming medicine (Benzodiazepine). These medicines impair your balance and double the risk of severe falls and broken bones.
rules.rationale: Sedation, motor incoordination, and blunted postural reflex recovery.
rules.source: AGS Beers Criteria 2023 / CDC STEADI Fall Guidelines

rules.title: Z-Hypnotic with Fall History · Nocturnal Awakening Fractures
rules.clinicalText: Z-drugs carry a fall risk hazard ratio comparable to long-acting benzodiazepines, especially upon nighttime awakening for micturition when residual ataxia is elevated.
rules.plainText: Sleeping pills (Z-drugs) cause residual morning unsteadiness and grogginess, leading to serious trips and falls when getting up at night.
rules.rationale: Rapid onset cerebellar-vestibular psychomotor slowing and nocturnal disorientation.

rules.title: Anticholinergic with Fall History · Sedation & Blurred Vision
rules.clinicalText: Anticholinergics cause pupillary dilation (mydriasis), blurred vision, orthostasis, and central sedation, directly contributing to trip-and-fall hazards in ambulatory older adults.
rules.plainText: This medication causes blurred vision, dizziness upon standing, and drowsiness, greatly increasing the danger of tripping and falling.
rules.rationale: Combination of cycloplegia, orthostatic hypotension, and central psychomotor impairment.

rules.title: Non-Selective Alpha-1 Blocker with Fall History · Orthostatic Syncope
rules.clinicalText: Peripherally acting alpha-1 blockers produce prominent first-dose and maintenance orthostatic hypotension, causing transient cerebral hypoperfusion and syncopal falls.
rules.plainText: Alpha-blockers can cause a sudden blood pressure drop when you stand up from a bed or chair, leading to dizziness, blackouts, and falls.
rules.rationale: Sympathetic vascular tone inhibition preventing reflex vasoconstriction on standing.

rules.title: Antipsychotic with Fall History · Extrapyramidal Gait Instability
rules.clinicalText: Antipsychotics cause dopamine receptor antagonism leading to drug-induced parkinsonism, muscle rigidity, akathisia, and orthostatic hypotension, compounding fall injury risk.
rules.plainText: Antipsychotic medications cause muscle stiffness, balance problems, and sudden lightheadedness that lead to dangerous falls in older adults.
rules.rationale: Extrapyramidal motor dysfunction combined with alpha-1 adrenergic blockade.

rules.title: Opioid Analgesic with Fall History · Central Sedation & Balance Loss
rules.clinicalText: Opioids produce central nervous system depression, dizziness, blurred vision, and cognitive clouding, directly increasing fall-related trauma and fractures in older adults.
rules.plainText: Opioid painkillers slow reflexes and cause dizziness and drowsiness. In patients with past falls, they significantly increase the chance of another injury.
rules.rationale: Central mu-opioid stimulation impairs vestibular and motor reflexes.

rules.title: Gabapentinoid with Fall History · Ataxia & Vestibular Dizziness
rules.clinicalText: Gabapentin and pregabalin inhibit presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels; dose-dependent somnolence, dizziness, and peripheral edema frequently precipitate falls in geriatric patients.
rules.plainText: Nerve pain medicines (Pregabalin / Gabapentin) commonly cause dizziness and unsteady walking. Extra caution and fall prevention measures are required.
rules.rationale: Presynaptic calcium channel modulation in cerebellar and vestibular pathways.

rules.title: Paracetamol in Hepatic Impairment · Glutathione Depletion Caution
rules.clinicalText: In severe liver disease or cirrhosis, hepatic glutathione reserves are depleted, reducing detoxication of the reactive metabolite NAPQI and increasing hepatotoxicity risk at standard doses.
rules.plainText: You have a liver condition and take Paracetamol. Because your liver's protective antioxidants are reduced, do not exceed 2,000 mg (2 grams) per day across all medicines.
rules.rationale: Impaired glucuronidation and depleted glutathione shift paracetamol metabolism toward toxic CYP2E1 oxidation.

rules.title: Statin in Active Hepatic Dysfunction · Transaminase Monitoring
rules.clinicalText: Statins undergo extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism. While safe in stable NAFLD/NASH, active acute hepatitis or decompensated cirrhosis requires cautious dosing and LFT monitoring.
rules.plainText: Your statin cholesterol medication is processed by your liver. In active liver issues, routine liver function blood tests are needed to ensure safety.
rules.rationale: Altered hepatic uptake transporters (OATP) and reduced CYP metabolism increase systemic statin bioavailability.
rules.source: National Lipid Association Statin Safety Guidance

rules.title: Long-Acting Benzodiazepine in Liver Disease · Hepatic Encephalopathy
rules.clinicalText: Long-acting benzodiazepines undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism (CYP) with prolonged elimination half-lives in cirrhosis, precipitating or worsening hepatic encephalopathy and coma.
rules.plainText: Long-acting sedatives take days to clear from an impaired liver, building up toxic levels that cause severe confusion, stupor, and hepatic encephalopathy.
rules.rationale: Severe clearance reduction of parent drug and active desmethyl metabolites.

rules.title: Methotrexate in Hepatic Disease · Progressive Fibrosis & Cirrhosis
rules.clinicalText: Methotrexate possesses intrinsic hepatotoxic potential, inducing stellate cell activation, portal tract inflammation, and progressive liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.
rules.plainText: Methotrexate can cause progressive scarring and liver damage. It is strictly contraindicated in patients with significant pre-existing liver disease.
rules.rationale: Metabolic accumulation of polyglutamated metabolites in hepatocytes inducing fibrogenesis.

rules.title: Oral Anticoagulant in Liver Disease · Supratherapeutic Bleeding Risk
rules.clinicalText: Impaired hepatic synthesis of baseline clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X) coupled with reduced drug clearance produces unpredictable, supratherapeutic anticoagulation and catastrophic bleeding.
rules.plainText: Your liver naturally produces the proteins that help your blood clot. Taking blood thinners with liver disease creates an extreme risk of severe internal bleeding.
rules.rationale: Additive synthetic liver failure and impaired pharmacological clearance.

rules.title: NSAID with Peptic Ulcer History · Severe Recurrent Perforation Risk
rules.clinicalText: Systemic COX-1 inhibition depletes cytoprotective gastric mucosal prostaglandins, leading to high rates of recurrent peptic ulceration, life-threatening gastrointestinal hemorrhage, and perforation.
rules.plainText: You have a history of stomach ulcers or gastrointestinal bleeding. NSAID pain relievers directly attack your stomach lining and can trigger severe bleeding ulcers.
rules.rationale: Depletion of gastric mucosal bicarbonate and mucus protective barriers.
rules.source: ACG Clinical Guideline: Bleeding Peptic Ulcer / AGS Beers 2023

rules.title: Aspirin with Peptic Ulcer History · Gastric Mucosal Erosion
rules.clinicalText: Aspirin produces direct topical chemical injury to gastric mucosa and irreversible platelet inhibition, dramatically elevating the risk of severe upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
rules.plainText: Aspirin irritates the stomach lining and prevents blood clotting. With your ulcer history, you must take stomach-protective medicine (PPI) alongside or consult your doctor.
rules.rationale: Dual topical acid injury and systemic irreversible platelet COX-1 inhibition.

rules.title: Corticosteroid with Ulcer History · Impaired Mucosal Healing
rules.clinicalText: Glucocorticoids impair fibroblast proliferation and capillary endothelial growth, delaying ulcer healing and predisposing patients to ulcer reactivation and perforation.
rules.plainText: Steroids slow down your stomach lining's ability to heal and protect itself, increasing ulcer risk in patients with prior ulcer history.
rules.rationale: Anti-inflammatory suppression of tissue repair and angiogenesis.

rules.title: Anticoagulant with Ulcer History · Severe Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage
rules.clinicalText: Full-dose anticoagulation in patients with active or recent peptic ulceration produces severe, potentially fatal hemorrhage from unhealed vascular lesions in the stomach or duodenum.
rules.plainText: Blood thinners with an active or recent stomach ulcer can cause massive internal bleeding. Immediate medical evaluation and gastroprotection are critical.
rules.rationale: Systemic hemostatic suppression unmasks bleeding from underlying mucosal defects.

rules.title: Thiazide Diuretic in Gout · Hyperuricemia & Severe Flare Trigger
rules.clinicalText: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics compete with uric acid for organic anion transporters in the proximal tubule, reducing urate clearance and precipitating acute gouty flares.
rules.plainText: Thiazide water pills stop your kidneys from getting rid of uric acid, which can trigger painful acute gout attacks in your joints.
rules.rationale: Enhanced renal proximal tubular urate reabsorption secondary to volume contraction and OAT competition.
rules.source: ACR Guideline for the Management of Gout / STOPP Criteria v3
